newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Some key facts on Slovenia as nation votes.
newsitem.headline: Some key facts on Slovenia as nation votes.

text.p: Slovenians voted on Sunday in their second general election since declaring independence from Yugoslavia in 1991. These are some key facts about Slovenia.
POPULATION: 1.99 million (1995), of which around 90 percent are Slovene with small numbers of ethnic Serbs, Croats, Albanians, Hungarians and Italians. Some 1.5 million are eligible to vote.
LANGUAGES: Official language is Slovene. Hungarian and Italian are recognised as minority languages.
RELIGION: Around three quarters of the population is Roman Catholic.
AREA: Total area is 20,250 square km (7,800 square miles). The northernmost of the former Yugoslav republics, it is bordered by Austria, Croatia, Hungary and Italy.

GOVERNMENT: Slovenia, a democratic republic, has a single legislature, the 90-seat National Assembly. The 40-member National Council has a mainly advisory function but may veto decisions of the National Assembly.
ECONOMY: Gross domestic product is expected to expand by three to four percent by the end of 1996. GDP increased 3.52 percent in 1995 -- making it by far the best performer in former Yugoslavia.
Agriculture accounts for around five percent of GDP, services for 25 percent and industry for 38 percent.
Credit agency Dun and Bradstreet gave Slovenia an unchanged DB3a credit rating for October, placing it behind the Czech Republic and ahead of Poland.
Annual inflation accelerated to 9.7 percent in October from 9.4 percent in September. The government has forecast inflation will stay below 10 percent to year end.
Unemployment rose to 13.5 percent in August from 13.3 percent in July.

Slovenia signed an association agreement with the European Union (EU) in June and has set its sights on joining the EU by 2001. It is also a strong contender to be among the first former communist states to join the NATO military alliance.

MODERN HISTORY: Slovenia was the first of Yugoslavia's six republics to hold free elections in 1990. Then the pro-independence, centre-right DEMOS coalition ended 45 years of communist rule and put Slovenia on the road to secession.

The republic voted for independence in a referendum in December 1990. It declared itself independent in June the following year, drawing the ire of the Yugoslav army which sent tanks to try to take control of its international borders.

Sixty-four people were killed before Slovenia signed a ceasefire agreement on July 7, 1991. It pushed ahead with its independence drive in October that year and introduced its own currency, the tolar, the same month.
Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek, once president of Yugoslavia, and his centre-left Liberal Democrats (LDS) formed a coalition government after Slovenia's last elections in 1992.
Latest opinion polls give the LDS 15.3-21.8 percent support. In 1992 they won a third of the vote. Coalition partners the Christian Democrats have 6.1 percent backing.
The rightist People's Party has 8.9-9.9 percent, ahead of the Social Democrats on eight percent. The United List of Social Democrats, the former communist party, has 4.7-6.8 percent.
